assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting changed how trade is modelled, measured and taught. It shifted the focus from industries and countries to firms, and it added new gains-from-trade channels (reallocation, selection) and new welfare and policy analysis. It has spawned a very large empirical literature on firm-level data, and the framework is now the standard workhorse in international economics.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) on exports versus FDI, and Helpman's wider work on trade with imperfect competition and firm organisation, complete the intellectual line. Redding is credited on the list but is more a later consolidator and quantifier, so he is left out. Empirical precursors on exporter premia (e.g. Bernard and Jensen) are not on the list, which makes attribution somewhat uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Over two decades since the core papers. The model's predictions have been tested repeatedly in firm-level data, and its extensions are well established. It is mature, and the field has not yet been recognised by the prize in this form.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to include an empirical pioneer of exporter heterogeneity.
Helpman also appears under B049, which could dilute or complicate his credit.
Some quantitative-trade critics argue the welfare gains from selection are smaller than the original theory suggests.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China-shock evidence reshaped understanding of wage inequality, polarisation and the local labour-market costs of trade and automation. The work is also highly influential in policy debates and links labour economics with trade.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task approach and the trade-shock work. Hanson (with Autor and Dorn) drives the China shock evidence, and Katz is the long-run anchor on skill demand and supply and wage structure. Dorn is a real co-author of the trade-shock papers and is omitted only because of the three-name limit. The task framework also owes much to Acemoglu, Goldin and others who are not credited and who were recently honoured.
assessment.maturity: The papers date from 2003 to 2013 and have been replicated and extended in many countries. Some debate remains over the persistence and magnitude of the effects, but the core findings have held up.
uncertainties: Overlap with recent prizes for labour, technology and inequality (Goldin 2023, Acemoglu 2024) may crowd out this topic.
Dorn's exclusion from the three-name selection is a real attribution cost.
Interpreting the China shock as a pure trade effect remains contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficient discrete-choice demand estimation with endogenous prices made it practical to measure market power, merger effects and welfare in differentiated-product markets. It underlies modern empirical IO, antitrust analysis and many applications in trade, health and environmental economics. The impact on methodology and practice is large and lasting.
assessment.attribution: The BLP (1995) paper is the core contribution, which supports Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes as a natural trio. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are credited for the wider structural IO agenda (entry, dynamics), but their roles are less sharply tied to the central estimator.
assessment.maturity: Over thirty years of continuous use, with extensive refinements and robust computational practice. Very mature.
uncertainties: There is a trade-off between honouring the BLP method and the broader structural IO agenda, which affects who is recognised.
Critiques of identification and numerical implementation exist but have not displaced the approach.
As an IO specialist I may weight this field more heavily than other members would, so the ranking should be read with that in mind.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Weak-instrument diagnostics and identification-robust inference corrected a widespread practical problem in IV estimation. They changed applied standards across labour, macro and development economics, and the contribution is methodological rather than a discovery about the economy.
assessment.attribution: Staiger and Stock (1997) is the foundation for the weak-instrument asymptotics. Andrews contributed general theory and inference procedures, and Moreira and Yogo made the key conditional-test and critical-value contributions. Bound, Jaeger and Baker, and Nelson and Startz, are important precursors who are not credited. Stock also appears in B006, so the credit is partly shared.
assessment.maturity: Developed from the 1990s through the 2010s and now routine in applied work, so it is mature. However, the 2021 IV and LATE recognition has already covered some of the neighbouring ground.
uncertainties: The field-level overlap with the 2021 prize may reduce the appetite for another instrumental-variables award.
The credit is spread over five names, and precursors are missing.
Methodological advances are sometimes judged to rank below substantive discoveries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The intertemporal, microfounded open-economy framework (the 'Redux' model and the book Foundations of International Macroeconomics) reshaped policy analysis in international macroeconomics. The exchange-rate disconnect puzzles define a large research agenda, and Rogoff also helped shape the debate on exchange-rate volatility and policy.
assessment.attribution: Obstfeld and Rogoff are an exceptionally clean pair, and their joint work is the core of the field. Rogoff's other credits (B022 with Reinhart) add breadth but also dilute attribution. Related contributions by Dornbusch, Mussa and others are acknowledged only through earlier prizes or deaths.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from the 1990s. Its practical success is more mixed, since the disconnect puzzles remain open and the framework was later superseded in part by dominant-currency and global-financial-cycle ideas. The influence is long-standing.
uncertainties: The puzzles that give the work its fame remain unsolved, which could be read either as a strength or as unfinished business.
Later work on dominant-currency pricing and invoicing (Gopinath and others, not credited here) has shifted the empirical consensus.
Because my own research touches pass-through and invoicing currency, I may be overly familiar with the strengths and weaknesses of this literature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Double/debiased machine learning, causal forests and related methods let researchers estimate treatment effects and heterogeneity with high-dimensional data under valid inference. The methods are spreading quickly through applied economics and into policy and industry.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov (with co-authors on double machine learning and high-dimensional inference), Athey (with Imbens and Wager on tree-based methods and policy learning) and Wager (causal forests) are the main drivers. Imbens, already a laureate, and Belloni, Hansen and others are important co-authors who are not credited, so attribution is clearly contested.
assessment.maturity: Most key results date from 2016 to 2020. Adoption is fast, but the long-run influence and robustness in practice are less well tested than for the older candidates.
uncertainties: It is probably too early to judge the lasting effect of these methods.
Overlap with Imbens's 2021 prize and the rapid movement of the field could make it hard to draw a clean credit boundary.
Chernozhukov also appears in B037, and Athey in B029, which spreads their credit across topics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Combining optimal-tax theory with credible estimates of behavioural responses (elasticity of taxable income, sufficient statistics) turned public finance into an empirically grounded policy science. It has direct influence on tax design and public debate.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod's work on taxable income and avoidance, Saez's work on the elasticity and optimal top rates, and Chetty's sufficient-statistics programme are each distinctive. The roots in Feldstein (deceased) and the optimal-tax tradition of Mirrlees and Diamond are only partly reflected here. Saez and Chetty also appear in other candidates (B036, B050), which spreads their credit.
assessment.maturity: The work spans the 1990s to the 2010s. It is largely mature, but the size of the elasticities and their policy relevance remain debated.
uncertainties: Elasticity estimates vary widely with setting, and the relationship with avoidance and evasion behaviour is still disputed.
Younger contributors (including Stantcheva) may only be fully assessed later.
Credit overlaps across several of the long-list entries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore's model of collateral constraints and credit cycles explains how small shocks are amplified and persist through asset prices and credit limits. It gave macroeconomics a core mechanism for financial amplification that became central after the 2008 crisis and has shaped both research and central-bank thinking.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) is the key paper, which makes the pair a clean choice. Gertler and Gilchrist's financial-accelerator work is the empirical and quantitative complement, and Bernanke, who shared the 2022 prize for work on banks and financial crises, is the main other pioneer.
assessment.maturity: Nearly thirty years of influence, with widespread extensions and a large literature on borrowing constraints and macroprudential policy. It is mature.
uncertainties: The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig) overlaps in subject matter.
A smaller body of work by the two laureates themselves than other candidates, although each paper is very influential.
Whether the committee would also want Gertler included for the quantitative accelerator.
